claims.text: Tailored microstructure in chromium- and nickel-alloyed steels promotes preferential nucleation and growth of a coherent Cr/Ni-rich passive oxide film.
The Cr/Ni-rich passive oxide film is more resistant to chemical attack than the film on the baseline steel.
The Cr/Ni-rich passive oxide film is more resistant to radiation-induced degradation than the film on the baseline steel.
Greater passive-film resistance to chemical and radiation-induced degradation enhances the steel's overall corrosion resistance.
Increasing Cr and Ni levels contributes to an alloy state favorable for corrosion resistance.
Controlled grain-boundary density fosters localized compositional segregation and precipitate formation.
Grain-boundary density and localized compositional segregation facilitate rapid nucleation of a protective Cr/Ni-rich oxide layer.
The uniformity and chemical stability of the passive film limit further oxidation.
The passive film resists degradation under combined high temperature, aggressive corrosive conditions, and radiation exposure.
Relative to the baseline steel, the advanced steel will form a significantly thicker passive oxide film.
Relative to the baseline steel, the advanced steel will form a more uniform passive oxide film.
Relative to the baseline steel, the advanced steel will exhibit lower corrosion current density.
Relative to the baseline steel, the advanced steel will exhibit higher electrochemical impedance.
Relative to the baseline steel, the advanced steel will undergo less degradation during prolonged exposure.
The proposed mechanism applies at approximately 300 degrees Celsius in aggressive acidic or alkaline media containing aggressive ions and under radiation representative of PWR operation.
A standard carbon or less-alloyed steel lacks the optimized microstructural features and high Cr/Ni content of the advanced steel.
